en: While his final journey is near,
His eyes have reddened like a raven’s,
His swan-white beard has grown long,
His remaining eye festers,
And his chest wheezes.
That accursed Bakay Khan—
Before his head enters the grave,
Before his soul reaches the earth—
Still devises perfect counsels
And will not abandon his mischief.
For Bakay’s many offenses,
I will make him taste misery;
I myself will give his punishment.
I will strip him and bend his back,
Load him upon a yellow gelded camel,
And heap boiling anguish upon him.
I will make eighty powerful wrestlers
Use Bakay as their kökbörü carcass
Three times each week;
I will have fools maul him,
And, granting Bakay no counsel,
I will make him weary of life.
In Bakay’s old age
I myself will settle his account;
I will beat out his ancient demon.
I will devise a superior stratagem
And somehow take the head
Of arrogant, deathless Bakay.
I will heap humiliation upon him like sheep;
I will gather without exception
All the descendants and people of Manas,
Grind them to stone dust,
And do as I please.
Massed black Jediger,
Come, every last one!” he shouted,
Calling their fiercest men.
Then Kanchoro,
Summoning them all to come, said:
“Brave Kyyaz of the Jediger,
You, their hero, stand here;
You resourceful, wise
Champion stand here;
You who boldly enter battle,
Khan of the massed black Jediger,
You stand here.
All you seasoned men who know the people,
All of you stand here;
All you farsighted men,
You long-eared listeners,
You strong men who know the distant future,
You strong men who know what is near;
You broad-chested lions,
You heroes who do not grieve
Though both feet burn in fire—
Turn and come here!
You unshaken lions,
You fortunate heroes on the road,
You mighty black Jediger,
My tigers, come here!
Believe the words of Kanchoro Khan,
All you people;
Your khan will speak now—
People, now behold!
Kanchoro who governs the people—
You know, great nation,
Kanchoro’s renown
And fierce Aychürök’s quarrel.
Will Kyyaz Khan lie still
Without taking fierce Aychürök,
That woman Aychürök,
That glinting infidel,
She who is famed as beautiful?
Did the settled Kyrgyz not witness
The strife she caused?
Toltoy Khan was to take her,
But the madman burned to death
And met his end through Külchoro.
Because of that former affair,
Because of fierce Aychürök,
Many khojas and khans died;
All who grappled with them died,
And many humble souls died too.
Spears were bundled and heaped;
Beginning with old Tölök,
How many were slaughtered together
And scattered abroad!
The camps of the Jediger people
Were broken and scattered;
Their wives were left widows.
No trace remained,
No tidings of the Jediger;
Only their willows remained upon the land,
Their children left as orphans.
How many of their khans were killed!
When you met face to face,
Many of your lives were destroyed.
Seeking to take fierce Chürök,
All of you were massacred.
Your turn has come: will you not
Settle your quarrel, Jediger?
Will you not slaughter
The enemy fallen into your hands, Jediger?
Will you not inflict
A singular, exacting calamity, Jediger?
Will you not avenge
The true grievance of the dead, Jediger?
Your chance has come into your hands—
Do you not see it, Jediger?
Will you not divide among yourselves
The bloodthirsty lord’s wives and children, Jediger?
Will you not give Kanchoro
Whomever he desires, Jediger?
Will you not submit to the decree
Spoken by your khan, Jediger?
Will you not find
Countless riches and abundant spoils, Jediger?
Will you not raid
Semetey Khan’s stronghold, Jediger?
Will you not beat out
The Kyrgyz madness, Jediger?
Will you not unleash
A dreadful affliction and great slaughter, Jediger?
And the fierce woman Aychürök—
Will you not take that proud woman as spoil,
Jediger?
Will you not boast throughout your lands,
Raise a clamor, and hold
A great feast for this, Jediger?
Will you not gather every nation
From Jeti-Özön, Jediger?
Will you not slaughter countless livestock
For the feast, Jediger?
Will you not cut her in two
And leave her for Kyyaz, Jediger?
Your khojas in white turbans,
Your mullahs who recite their lessons,
Your elders who can fly,
And all who know their crafts—
Will you not gather them, Jediger?
For your lord Kyyaz,
Cutting shares in this way,
Will you not carve them, Jediger?
Chürök, beautiful as the sun—
Grief and calamity follow behind her;
Such is Chürök’s nature.
With her white breasts exposed,
Her dawn pale as a mountain sheep,
Her eyes shining like a camel calf’s,
Will you not drive her
Among sixty wrestlers and eighty men,
Making a spectacle for all
That ears may hear and eyes may see,
And heap on Aychürök’s head
Affliction and strife no nation has witnessed,
Jediger?
Beautiful Aychürök is your captive;
That is Kanchoro’s counsel.
Brave Kyyaz, struck by a man’s curse,
If you wish, she is your wife;
If her widowhood is truly disputed,
She is in truth your own spouse,
The wife from your village in Jeti-Özön,
Won through contention in Talas,
Whom you carried off as your wife.
How is it, Kyyaz, that you sank
Into merry games and great feasts?
How is it, Kyyaz, that you lie there,
Regarding Chürök as a maiden?
How is it, Kyyaz, that you raised Kanchoro
And made him khan?
How is it, Kyyaz, that you feast
On merry games and entertainment?
Having won the stronghold and mounted the throne,
Swelling with great fortune,
How is it, Kyyaz, that you sank into it?
How is it, Kyyaz, that you lie
In broad pleasure and great amusement?
That scheming infidel—
That woman Aychürök—
Know this that I tell you;
You are a man, Kyyaz, heed my words!
When you take Aychürök
And carry her to your village,
One woman grasping at your collar
Must not destroy a whole cliff;
One woman raising a quarrel
Must not ruin all the livestock.
The two reins and single lead-rope—
Without treating Chürök merely as a woman,
Place them wholly in her hands.
Submit to whatever
That shimmering infidel demands;
Do the deeds she tells you.
For the fierce woman who overcame you,
Until seven full years have passed,
Keep doing whatever she says.
Set up a gilded throne,
Plant a garden of plane trees around it;
Let no willow fail to leaf.
Let nightingales and birds of every kind
Perch in the tower and sing expertly.
Let no resentment remain
Inside the ill-fated infidel,
The fierce woman Chürök.
From beneath every plane tree
Let a spring boil up and overflow;
Upon every plane tree
Let mournful creatures sing and trill,
And whoever hears them weep tears.
Build her a palace for promenades.
Brave Kyyaz, giant of the Jediger,
If you are a man, if you are a lion,
Take these words to heart.
Gather your heroes and hold games;
Hold the games of Kanchoro Khan.
Carry out the words of a wise hero;
Without discarding a single word,
Do exactly as I say.
I tell you ten thousand words—know them;
Accursed Kyyaz, heed my tongue!
Prepare all four kinds of livestock,
And deceive Chürök, who struck from above,
With all your wealth.
This woman Aychürök—
What does that shimmering infidel
Possess, and what does she lack?
She is good and radiantly beautiful,
And she also has humanity;
She is a true sorceress and witch,
And has an infidel’s nature too.
This is what I tell you, brave Kyyaz:
Do not raise your whip and strike her;
Do not take the daylight from beneath her;
Do not leave yourself in such torment.
Do not rage at her in manly pride;
Never curse or revile her.
That sorcerous infidel,
The enchanted woman Chürök—
If you should accidentally wound her heart,
If you should quarrel by mischance,
If you should fight by accident—
She knows on Friday where a bird has flown,
And on the holy night she knows its course.
She has skimmed the surface of the earth,
Flying as she roamed
The whole world under moon and sky.
That gracious, beautiful infidel,
That woman Aychürök,
Has no region she has not known intimately,
No man she has left untested,
No region over which she has not flown,
No man she has failed to visit.
She has roamed the whole world,
A serving woman who knows six spans,
And knows all the world
That serving woman has seen it all while roaming;
